summary: Light by Lake Michigan near Whitehall, Michigan: a pier beacon from 1872, the on-shore tower of 1875-76, keeper William Robinson 1872-1919, and a museum since 1970.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The different years are different structures: 1872 is the pier-head beacon, with William Robinson first keeper (Lakeshore Keepers); 1875 is the on-shore tower the archive records as established; 1876 is when the on-shore fourth-order lens was first shown (Lakeshore Keepers). The archive's lens field gives 1875, which this story reports as a conflict.
The archive spells her Frances Johnson for 1944-1954. Lakeshore Keepers calls her Frances Johnson Marshall. The name variants are kept in the keeper notes.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: (1) The Lakeshore Keepers history summarises Thomas A. Tag's White River Light Station (1996), which I could not read; its facts are footnoted to Lakeshore Keepers as a secondary source. Verify against Tag or the Fruitland Township archive before the keepers index links any name. (2) Thomas Robinson: the archive has a first assistant of 1880-1882; Lakeshore has a son of that name as assistant 1877-1919. Not merged; a human should decide. (3) Automation: Lakeshore says the main tower light was automated in 1945; the archive lists principal keepers to 1959 (Andrew Newald 1954-1959). Unresolved. (4) Lens year: the archive field gives 1875 and Lakeshore gives April 1876. (5) Frances Johnson: the archive lists Frances Johnson; Lakeshore Keepers calls her Frances Johnson Marshall and gives the claim 'last female lighthouse keeper in Michigan', which I could not check. Wikipedia's lead gives 'Frances Marshall' and the same claim; Wikipedia is not cited. (6) The USLHS history block (1871 construction of the pier beacon, 1874 appropriation of $15,000, 1876 on-shore light, 1902 lens reduction, 1918 electric, 1960 deactivated, 1965 Fruitland proposal) is in the cached HTML but not in the text check_quotes reads, so it is not quoted; the 1871 and 1874 facts are therefore left out of the story. (7) NRHP: the cached national-register list (data/raw/nrhp/national-register-listed.xlsx) has no entry for White River Light, and no nomination was found. (8) Newspapers: two Chronicling America searches for Michigan (keeper names, 'White River' light) returned nothing relevant; the Official Register was not searched. (9) The Life-Saving Service station at White River is a separate federal station; the story describes its crews as 'the station crew' and does not give it a station record. No LSS station record for White River exists in data/stations; consider linking one. (10) Life-Saving dating: the 1888 volume covers the fiscal year ending 30 June 1888 (so 25 October falls in 1887); the 1889 volume covers the year ending 30 June 1889 (so 4 April is 1889). (11) The 2025 Light List Volume VII (local copy) has no White River entry, consistent with discontinuance; not cited. (12) Wikipedia says 1872 South Pier and 1876 Main Tower; Wikidata first_lit 1872 is the pier beacon. (13) Atmosphere: the 1888 ice and storm scenes are the Life-Saving Service's own words; the 1864 rule is labelled general context. (14) Characteristic conflict: the 1893 Board report (scan p. 172) records the change on 12 December 1892 to a red flash every forty seconds, but the Board's 1899 list (scan p. 47) still gives 'a red flash every minute'. The story reports the 1899 list and does not explain it; Lakeshore Keepers says the rotation was changed again in 1901. (15) Electric change: the Commissioner's 1919 entry sits under the heading 'acetylene or other lights changed from oil-wick lights' for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1919; it is not a list of lights in commission on that date, and the story says so. The 1918 Bulletin index also lists 'White River, change in illuminant' (not cited). (16) Building material: the archive says the tower is limestone; Lakeshore Keepers says the foundation is limestone and the walls are yellow Michigan brick. The story states both. (17) Scan pages were checked with corpus.py page against the OCR page index. The corpus grep labels for the 1888 volume gave scan 196 and 285 for the October 25 and April 7 passages; the page index places them at scan 153 (printed 147) and 265 (printed 259), so the story uses 153 and 265. (18) The 1864 rules are catalogued as 1864 by the Internet Archive; the story says 'labeled 1864' and does not claim a printing date.
